contentBlocks.body: Shared mutable state plus more than one thread gives race conditions. `count++` looks atomic but is read, add, then write; two threads can read the same value and one increment is lost. `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` is not safe for concurrent writes at all and can corrupt its internal state. A singleton service in ASP.NET Core is shared by every concurrent request, so these bugs show up in web apps, not only in explicitly parallel code.
Pick the lightest tool that makes the operation atomic:

- `Interlocked.Increment/Add/Exchange/CompareExchange` for a single numeric field or reference. Lock-free and very cheap.
- `lock (gate) { ... }` for multi-step invariants: check-then-act, or updating two fields together. Keep the body short and never `await` inside it (the compiler forbids it). Use `SemaphoreSlim(1, 1)` with `WaitAsync` for async code.
- `ConcurrentDictionary`, `ConcurrentQueue`, `ConcurrentBag` for shared collections, using their atomic compound methods.

A detail interviewers probe: `GetOrAdd(key, factory)` and `AddOrUpdate` can run the factory **more than once** under contention; only one result is stored, but the side effects of the others still happen. For expensive or side-effecting creation, store a `Lazy<T>`: `GetOrAdd(key, k => new Lazy<T>(() => Create(k))).Value`. Also note that `if (!dict.ContainsKey(k)) dict[k] = v;` is still a check-then-act race, even on a ConcurrentDictionary.

A test that passes with a plain Dictionary under Parallel.ForEach proves nothing. Races are timing-dependent, so thread-safety must be argued from the code: every shared write must be atomic or protected.

knowledgeItems.prompt: Several threads run `_count++` on a shared int field. What is the fix with the least overhead?

payload.explanation: Interlocked performs the read-add-write as one atomic CPU operation. volatile only affects visibility and ordering; it does not make ++ atomic.

knowledgeItems.prompt: What is surprising about the value factory passed to ConcurrentDictionary.GetOrAdd?

choices: It can run more than once for the same key when threads race, although only one value is stored
It always runs while a global lock is held
It runs on a background thread
It is never called if the key is a string
payload.answer: It can run more than once for the same key when threads race, although only one value is stored
payload.explanation: The dictionary does not lock around your delegate. Wrap expensive or side-effecting creation in Lazy<T> so it runs once.
